item.title: The configuration
item.description:
One HCL file, or a directory of them: --config /etc/authn-bridge reads every *.hcl there in name order and merges them, and --config may be given more than once. The configuration is read at start and never again.

issuer = "https://login.example.org" # https; compared whole by every relying party
listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # the default: plain HTTP behind a TLS proxy
signing_key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/oidc.key" # authn-bridge keygen --key
subject_salt_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/salt" # authn-bridge keygen --salt; never change it
disabled_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/disabled.json"
certificates_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/certificates.json"

saml {
 key_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.key"
 cert_file = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/saml.crt"
 metadata_url = "https://pub.federation.renater.fr/metadata/fer/idps.xml"
 metadata_cert_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/metadata-signature-2026.pem"
 metadata_fingerprint = "68:2F:20:58:41:9E:D0:79:EB:FE:3C:27:D6:A4:A4:09:39:6F:AE:3F:10:5F:22:EA:04:0F:04:F3:78:2D:5C:C0"
}

state {
 driver = "sqlite" # or postgres, mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn"
}

client "my-app" {
 secret_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/my-app.secret" # absent: a public client
 redirect_uris = ["https://app.example.org/callback"]
}

What is required is issuer, signing_key_file, subject_salt_file, a saml block with the five keys above, and at least one client. Everything else has a default or is off.

check, before a restart

check reads the configuration the way the server does, loads every key it names, fetches the federation’s metadata, and says what would be served:

$ authn-bridge check --config etc/bridge.hcl
issuer http://127.0.0.1:28473
SAML entity http://127.0.0.1:28473/saml
tls none (a reverse proxy in front)
federation 1 IdPs, 1 usable here, valid until 2026-10-17T19:16:33Z
client sftp (public, public subject, audience [sftp])
client efp (public, public subject, audience [efp])
client nfs (public, public subject, audience [nfs])

Usable here leaves out an IdP that saml { idps } does not list, and one the admin API has disabled: with the institution above disabled, the same command prints federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here. An idps entry the federation does not list is refused here, though the server would start with it:

federation 1 IdPs, 0 usable here, valid until 2026-10-17T19:16:33Z
authn-bridge: idps names "https://idp.nowhere.example/idp", which the federation does not list

authn-bridge metadata prints the SAML metadata to register with the federation. See the federation side.

The top level

key default
issuer the provider’s name and the base of every URL. https, or http on a loopback host for testing; no query, no fragment; a trailing / is dropped
listen 127.0.0.1:8080 the public listener
cert_file, key_file serve TLS from these files, re-read when they change; together or not at all
acme serve TLS with a certificate from an ACME CA instead (below); not with cert_file
signing_key_file RSA, signs ID tokens (RS256); a P-256 key here is refused
access_token_key_file the signing key a P-256 key that signs access tokens ES256; refused if it is the signing key
retired_signing_key_files keys that signed before: still published at /jwks, never used to sign
subject_salt_file at least 32 bytes
code_lifetime 1m at most ten minutes (RFC 6749 4.1.2)
token_lifetime 1h access tokens
id_token_lifetime 5m ID tokens
trusted_proxies addresses or prefixes whose X-Forwarded-For is believed
requests_per_minute 120 logins, device grants and ACS posts an address may start a minute; 0 turns the limit off
disabled_file where disabled people and institutions are kept; without it, disabling is refused
certificates_file every certificate and WireGuard key issued; required with ssh_ca, x509_ca or wireguard

The blocks:

block page
saml, claims the federation side
client below, and tokens
state below
ssh_ca, x509_ca certificates
app_passwords, wireguard tokens
ssf revocation
admin, metrics the admin API
acme below

A client

key default
secret_file the client secret, at least 16 characters; absent, a public client
redirect_uris compared exactly, except that a loopback URI may change port (RFC 8252); http only on loopback
audience the client ID what its access tokens are addressed to
subject public or pairwise: a different sub for this client (OIDC Core 8.1)
name the client ID shown on the device confirmation page
device false the device grant (RFC 8628); such a client needs no redirect URI
refresh_lifetime off refresh tokens, and how long after the login they end
pkce required or or_nonce, for a confidential client only: a nonce instead of PKCE
id_token_claims false copy the released claims into the ID token as well (opkssh needs it)
ssh_certificates, ssh_* SSH certificates
x509_certificates NFS client certificates
app_passwords may set the person’s application password
wireguard_keys, wireguard_peers WireGuard
ssf_receiver, ssf_subject_format a Shared Signals receiver

A client with no redirect URI must be a device client, an SSF receiver or a WireGuard gateway, or there is nothing it could do.

state: what a restart must not forget 

state {
 driver = "postgres" # sqlite, postgres or mysql
 dsn_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/state.dsn"
}

Refresh token families, the refresh tokens and the retired ones, the access tokens honoured at /userinfo and for certificates, the SAML assertions already accepted and the logins already answered, the SSF streams and their undelivered events: written through to one table, bridge_state (created if missing), and read at start. A refresh token is kept as its SHA-256, never as itself. Without the block they live in memory, and a restart logs everybody out.

A login in progress is not in it. It travels in its own cookie, sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key derived from the subject salt, so the browser can neither read nor change it.

acme 

acme {
 accept_terms_of_service = true # the operator's agreement; no default
 cache_dir = "/var/lib/authn-bridge/acme"
 email = "noc@example.org"
 # directory_url = "..." # Let's Encrypt by default
 # eab_key_id = "..." # External Account Binding (GÉANT TCS / HARICA)
 # eab_hmac_key_file = "/etc/authn-bridge/harica-eab.key"
 # http_listen = ":80" # http-01, and a redirect to https
 # directory_ca_file = "..." # a private ACME CA's own TLS
}

The certificate is for the issuer’s host. cache_dir holds private keys, and the provider refuses to start on one another user could reach or re-point.

What is refused at startup

Each of these is the output of authn-bridge check on a configuration that asked for it. The server refuses the same configurations.

An issuer, a redirect, a secret that leak:

authn-bridge: issuer "http://login.example.org": an issuer is https (http only on loopback, for testing)
authn-bridge: client "web": redirect URI "http://app.example.org/callback": a code sent over cleartext http is a code anybody on the path has
authn-bridge: client "web": a secret of 5 characters is a password somebody can guess
authn-bridge: code_lifetime = 15m0s: an authorization code lives ten minutes at most

A name any institution could claim:

authn-bridge: claims: username = "uid" is not held to an IdP's scopes, so any IdP of the federation could name anybody: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use eppn or subject_id
authn-bridge: claims: groups = "affiliation" carries no institution, so any IdP of the federation could grant any of its values: it needs saml { idps } to list exactly one IdP; with more, use scoped_affiliation

Something issued that could never be taken back:

authn-bridge: ssh_ca: certificates_file is required with ssh_ca or x509_ca: a certificate that is not recorded can never be revoked
authn-bridge: ssh_ca: validity = 200h0m0s: more than a week, and a certificate lives that long on every server its revocation has not reached
authn-bridge: ssf: needs a state block: a queue a restart empties loses revocations

A listener that should not be reachable:

authn-bridge: admin: control: listen address "127.0.0.1:9443" is TCP, which requires mutual TLS (loopback included: any local user can reach it); missing TLSCertFile, TLSKeyFile, ClientCAFile
authn-bridge: metrics: listen is the public listener; metrics have one of their own

A configuration that says one thing twice:

authn-bridge: saml: an external discovery service lists every IdP; with `idps` restricted, leave `discovery` out and this provider lists them itself
authn-bridge: client "sftp" is declared twice

The SSH profile’s own refusals are on certificates, and the federation’s on the federation side.

item.title: The configuration
item.description:
One file, /etc/authn-revokd/revokd.hcl by default (-config names another). It is read once, at start.

state_dir = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/state" # the verified copies: what orders the next list
refresh = "1m"

source "univ-a-ssh" {
 url = "https://login.univ-a.fr/ssh/krl" # and .../ssh/krl.sig beside it
 ssh_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-ssh.pub" # what the list must be signed by
}
source "univ-b-ssh" {
 url = "http://mirror.cluster.local:8080/univ-b-ssh" # a mirror: plain http is fine
 ssh_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-b-ssh.pub"
}
source "univ-a-x509" {
 url = "https://login.univ-a.fr/x509/crl"
 x509_ca = "/etc/authn-revokd/ca/univ-a-x509.pem"
}

output "sshd" { # sshd_config: RevokedKeys /var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl
 path = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/sshd.krl"
 sources = ["univ-a-ssh", "univ-b-ssh"] # merged into one file
}
output "tls" { # nginx: ssl_crl /var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl
 path = "/var/lib/authn-revokd/univ-a.crl"
 sources = ["univ-a-x509"]
 format = "pem"
}

# listen = "127.0.0.1:8080" # serve the verified lists: a mirror

The keys

key default
state_dir required, absolute; created 0700 if missing
refresh 1m how often every source is fetched, a second or more; each wait varies by a tenth either way, so a fleet does not stay in step
listen host:port: serve the verified lists, a mirror; ignored with -once

source "<name>": one list. The name is letters, digits, ., _ and -, not starting with a dot, at most 64 characters: it names a file in the state directory and a path of the mirror.

key
url https://, http:// or file://; a KRL’s signature is fetched from the same URL with .sig appended
ssh_ca the SSH CA’s public key, one authorized_keys line: a KRL source. A certificate is refused here
x509_ca the CA’s PEM certificate: a CRL source
max_age also refuse a list issued longer ago than this, besides its own expiry; refused on a source that feeds a CRL output
revoke_keys let this source’s list revoke plain keys in an output shared with other sources; KRL sources only

output "<name>": one file a server reads.

key
path absolute; written beside itself and renamed over
sources KRL sources, merged into one file; or exactly one CRL source
format der (the default) or pem; CRL outputs only
on_change a command and its arguments, run after the file changes, and again at every sync until it succeeds

One KRL for several CAs

RevokedKeys takes a single file before OpenSSH 10.3, so the KRL sources of an output are merged, and each list keeps its full effect on its own CA, and none on another:

  • Kept: its serials and key IDs, its sections that name no CA (scoped to its own), and its own CA key, which revokes all its certificates.
  • Left out, and logged: another CA’s section, and another CA’s key.
  • Plain user keys are left out when the output has more than one source, unless the source has revoke_keys = true. A KRL cannot scope a key to one CA: sshd checks a certificate’s own key against the file whoever signed it, so a key one CA names would lock its holder out under every CA of the file. An output with one source keeps them.

Each list is first merged alone. One that cannot be merged fails closed for its own CA only; the merged file expires with the first of its current inputs, so a reader that checks expiry sees authn-revokd stop.

The mirror

With listen, authn-revokd serves what it holds, from memory, never from the files a write may be half way through:
GET /<source> the list, with an ETag; If-None-Match answers 304
GET /<source>.sig a KRL’s signature; If-Match on another ETag answers 412
GET /healthz 200 ok, or 503 naming each source with no current list and each output that failed 
$ curl -s http://127.0.0.1:28474/healthz
ok
$ curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:28474/bridge-ssh
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=30
Content-Type: application/octet-stream
Etag: "5b1194d230399c2d1c5b0d904aa91101"
Date: Sat, 10 Oct 2026 19:19:20 GMT
Content-Length: 130
$ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -H 'If-Match: "stale"' http://127.0.0.1:28474/bridge-ssh.sig
412

A CRL source has no .sig (404). Mirrors chain: a mirror’s source can be another mirror, since every list verifies by itself. A slow upstream never blocks the mirror’s answers.

What is refused at start

Each of these exits 2 before anything is fetched:

authn-revokd: v/relative-state.hcl: state_dir "state": an absolute path
authn-revokd: v/refresh.hcl: refresh "500ms": a duration of a second or more
authn-revokd: v/both-ca.hcl: source "bridge-ssh": ssh_ca and x509_ca together: one source is one list
authn-revokd: v/sig-name.hcl: source "bridge-ssh.sig": a name that ends in .sig, or healthz, is a path the mirror already serves
authn-revokd: v/mixed.hcl: output "sshd" mixes KRL and CRL sources
authn-revokd: v/krl-format.hcl: output "sshd": format is for CRL outputs; a KRL is what sshd reads
authn-revokd: v/revoke-keys-crl.hcl: source "bridge-x509": revoke_keys is for a KRL source (ssh_ca): a CRL revokes its own CA's certificates only

So does a configuration that is not there:

$ authn-revokd -config nowhere.hcl -once
authn-revokd: nowhere.hcl: no such file or directory

Before v0.6.2 it was the HCL parser’s message: nowhere.hcl: <nil>: Failed to read file; The configuration file "nowhere.hcl" could not be read.

A CRL output also takes one source (a TLS server reads one CRL per issuer), and a CRL source with max_age is refused, because nothing could enforce it:

authn-revokd: v/crl-maxage.hcl: output "tls": source "bridge-x509" has a max_age, which a CRL output cannot enforce: the TLS server judges a CRL by its nextUpdate alone. Remove max_age, or ask the CA for a closer nextUpdate

A TLS server that loaded a CRL keeps it in memory until its nextUpdate, whatever authn-revokd writes.

The state directory is held to sshd’s StrictModes rule. Whoever can replace or remove its files decides which list comes next, and an emptied state lets a replayed older list in. So it may not be a symbolic link, writable by group or others, or owned by anybody but authn-revokd’s user or root. These exit 1:

authn-revokd: state_dir /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/state-wide is writable by its group or by others (mode -rwxrwxrwx): whoever can write there decides which list comes next
authn-revokd: state_dir /tmp/docs-patch-a2daf7c8/revokd/state-link is a symbolic link (L---------): whoever owns it decides where the state is; name the directory itself

item.title: Where the people come from
item.description:
A user block is the whole directory for a small site, or the service accounts a big one keeps out of its database. A site whose people are already in a database or in LDAP should not copy them into a second place that goes stale, so a users block reads them where they are. The users block is go-authn/directory’s hcldir, the same one go-fileshare reads: one directory is described the same way to both.

Written in the configuration 

user "alice" { password_file = "/etc/authnd/passwords/alice.pw" }

user "carol" {
 nt_hash = "…" # MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex
 authorized_keys = ["ssh-ed25519 AAAA… carol@laptop"] # published as sshPublicKey
}

group "staff" { members = ["alice", "carol"] }
field what it is
password the password, inline
password_file the same, read from a file (surrounding white space removed)
nt_hash MD4(UTF16LE(password)), 32 hex characters — for a site that holds that and not the password
totp_secret a base32 one-time-code secret, at least 128 bits; see a second factor
authorized_keys authorized_keys lines, published as sshPublicKey
authorized_keys_file the same, from a file

Refused at startup, naming the person:

  • password and password_file together — say which one;
  • password and nt_hash together — the hash is derived from the password, so two of them can disagree;
  • authorized_keys and authorized_keys_file together;
  • an nt_hash that is not 32 hex characters, an authorized_keys line that does not parse, a totp_secret under 128 bits;
  • the same user or group twice, and a group with no members.

A group member that no source knows is refused too, which is what catches a typo before it silently grants nothing:

$ authnd check cases/typo.hcl
authnd: group "staff" has "alise" in it, who is not in the configuration file

An nt_hash alone cannot bind

A person written with only nt_hash is published, can be handed to an SMB server through sambaNTPassword, and cannot bind to authnd itself: an LDAP simple bind sends the password, and an NT hash is not a way to check one here. bob below has only an NT hash, and the hash is that of the password sent:

$ ldapwhoami -x -H ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 -D uid=bob,ou=people,dc=example,dc=org -y bob.pwin
ldap_bind: Invalid credentials (49)

check says so, after the tables:

bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against

In a SQL database 

users "sql" {
 driver = "postgres" # or mysql (mariadb), or sqlite
 dsn_file = "/etc/authnd/pg.dsn" # required: a DSN may hold a password
 users = "select login, secret, nt_hash from staff" # required
 groups = "select team, member from team_members" # optional
}

The queries are yours, because a site’s people are already in that site’s shape. The users query’s columns are read by position: a name, then any of a password, an NT hash, SSH keys (one per line) and a one-time-code secret, in that order — up to five columns. A NULL is a credential that person does not have. A password column is compared as it is stored: authnd has no setting for a hashed column. The groups query returns a group name and a member, one row per membership.

driver accepts postgres (or postgresql, pgx), mysql (or mariadb) and sqlite (or sqlite3). The database is reached at startup, before anything listens, so one that is not answering stops the server where somebody is watching:

$ authnd check cases/nodb
authnd: users "sql": the postgres database is not answering: failed to connect to `user=authnd database=authnd`:
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused
127.0.0.1:1 (127.0.0.1): dial error: dial tcp 127.0.0.1:1: connect: connection refused

PostgreSQL on the same machine through its socket and peer authentication needs no password in the DSN: host=/run/postgresql dbname=authnd user=authnd. SQLite in the state directory: file:/var/lib/authnd/people.db.

A key that belongs to the other kind of block is refused rather than ignored:

$ authnd check cases/sqlwrongkey.hcl
authnd: users "sql" has base_dn in it, which belongs to an ldap block

In another LDAP directory 

users "ldap" {
 url = "ldaps://ldap.example.org"
 base_dn = "ou=people,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_dn = "cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org"
 bind_password_file = "/etc/authnd/upstream.pw"
}

url and base_dn are required. Where the people and groups are, and which attributes name them:

key default
user_filter (objectClass=posixAccount)
user_attribute uid
group_base_dn base_dn
group_filter (objectClass=posixGroup)
group_attribute cn
group_member_attribute memberUid
totp_attribute none: there is no standard attribute, and a guess would read nothing while looking like it had looked
start_tls false

sambaNTPassword and sshPublicKey are read under those names. Two things are refused before anything is opened:

$ authnd check cases/ldap-clear.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" would send every password to "ldap.example.org" in the clear: use ldaps://, or start_tls = true (RFC 4513 §5.1.3)
$ authnd check cases/ldap-cred.hcl
authnd: users "ldap" has credentials in its url, and a url is printed: use bind_dn with bind_password_file

ldap:// to a loopback address and ldapi:// are accepted: nobody is on the way.

A directory behind this one checks passwords by binding to it; it does not hand them over. Here one authnd fronts another, under a different base:

$ authnd check front2
ldap://127.0.0.1:3894, base dc=example,dc=net
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS
alice ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check uid and cn
bob ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check uid and cn
dora ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check uid and cn
eli ldap://127.0.0.1:3893 a password check uid and cn
svc-backup the configuration file a password uid and cn
GROUP MEMBERS
engineers dora and eli
staff alice, bob and dora
a bind carries a password
no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

A password check is enough for a bind, and is never enough for a Kerberos ticket or for SMB.

Order, and the one exception

Sources are asked in the order they are written, and the first one that knows a name owns it. The user blocks always come first, so a service account written down locally is not overridden by somebody with the same name in the database. Group membership is the union of every source: staff above has alice and bob from one file and dora from a database.

Two names that differ only by case are refused

A uid is compared ignoring case (RFC 4519 §2.39), and so is every DN, so Dora in the file and dora in a database are one name to LDAP and two people to anything that compares bytes — a password change by one would land on the other. Such a configuration does not start:

$ authnd check cases/case.hcl
authnd: "Dora" (from the configuration file) and "dora" (from a sqlite database) differ only by case, and an LDAP name does not tell them apart: a uid is compared ignoring case. Rename one of them

Read once

Every source is read once, at startup. A person added to the database, or a membership changed in the directory behind this one, is served after a restart, not before. That includes a password column in a database: it is read with the rest of the row. A directory behind this one is different only in that a bind is checked by binding to it, so a password changed there is the one that works. The other exception is a password a person changes through authnd itself, which is applied at once. There is no reload; see running it.

item.title: check, before you restart something people log in through
item.description:
authnd check /etc/authnd
authnd check --config a.hcl --config b.hcl

check reads the configuration exactly as the server does, opens everything the server opens before it listens — the files, the database, the directory behind this one, the identity provider’s discovery document, the TLS certificate and key, the keytab — and prints what would be published and to whom, without listening. It prints where every credential comes from and never what is in it. It exits 0 and ends with this configuration can be served, or exits 1 with the one sentence that stops the server.

A configuration that can be served

Two user blocks, a reader, and a SQLite database, in a directory of two files (authnd.hcl and people.hcl):

$ authnd check etc/authnd
ldap://127.0.0.1:3893, base dc=example,dc=org
USER FROM CAN PROVE PUBLISHED AS
alice the configuration file a password uid and cn
bob the configuration file an NT hash uid and cn
dora a sqlite database a password uid and cn
eli a sqlite database an NT hash uid and cn
GROUP MEMBERS
engineers dora and eli
staff alice, bob and dora
a bind carries a password
bob and eli cannot bind with a password: their sources hold only what an SMB server needs (an NT hash), which a bind cannot be checked against
cn=reader,dc=example,dc=org may search; every other bound client may not
sambaNTPassword is not published, so nothing here can authenticate an SMB session (NTLMv2 needs the password or its MD4, and a bind cannot answer it)
this configuration can be served

Reading it

The first line is the scheme, the address and the base: ldap://, ldaps://, or ldap+starttls:// — see TLS.

column
FROM the source that owns the name: the configuration file, a sqlite database (or postgres, mysql), or the url of a directory behind this one
CAN PROVE a password (held, so it can be compared and keys derived from it), a password check (another directory answers yes or no), an NT hash, N keys, a one-time-code secret, or nothing
PUBLISHED AS the attributes the entry carries: always uid and cn; sambaNTPassword when publish_nt_hash is on and the person has one or a password it can be derived from; sshPublicKey when there are keys

The lines after the tables say what a person needs to know before relying on the configuration:

  • what a bind carries: a password, or, with an mfa block, a password with a 6-digit code after it; with an oidc block, where tokens come from and over what;
  • who cannot bind with a password at all: people known only by an NT hash — see people;
  • who may search: the readers, or no reader is declared: nothing may search, and binds are not affected;
  • whether sambaNTPassword is published, and over what — see publish_nt_hash;
  • with a kerberos block, the realm and who can and who cannot be issued a ticket, with the reason;
  • with an mfa block, who has no second factor, and so cannot bind with a password; with an oidc block beside it the line adds that a token whose amr names two kinds still can;
  • a group that names somebody no source has.

That last one is published as it stands — memberUid is a string, and a front for one system legitimately carries names another one owns — but it is said, because the other reading is a typo. Here the database’s team_members table has a row for zoe, who is nobody here:

GROUP MEMBERS
engineers dora, eli and zoe
staff alice, bob and dora
engineers names zoe, who has no entry here: the group is published as it stands, and nothing here can prove them

(A group block naming a stranger is refused outright; see people.)

What it refuses

Each of these stops check and the server alike, with exit status 1. They are on the pages where they belong; a few, as printed:

$ authnd check cases/nobody.hcl
authnd: there is nobody here: name a user, or a users block reading a database or a directory
$ authnd check cases/nthash-clear.hcl
authnd: publish_nt_hash needs cert_file and key_file: an NT hash IS the credential, and 0.0.0.0:3893 is not loopback, so it would cross a network in the clear
$ authnd check cases/krb-mfa.hcl
authnd: kerberos and mfa together: the mfa block asks every bind for a password AND a code, and a kinit carries only the password -- this KDC has no second-factor pre-authentication, so a realm here would accept one factor where the mfa block demands two. Remove one of the blocks
$ authnd check empty
authnd: empty has no .hcl files in it
$ authnd
authnd: no configuration: give a .hcl file or a directory of them

The certificate, the keytab, and the one thing it cannot see

A certificate that does not load and a keytab without krbtgt/REALM are refused by check, in the words the server would use:

$ authnd check cases/badcert
authnd: the certificate: open tls/missing.pem: no such file or directory
$ authnd check cases/nokrbtgt
authnd: kdc: the keytab has no krbtgt key for this realm: matching key not found in keytab. Looking for "krbtgt/EXAMPLE.ORG" realm: EXAMPLE.ORG kvno: 0 etype: 18

What check cannot know without listening is whether the ports are free. A second server on the same Kerberos address passes check and is refused at start:

$ authnd --config cases/realm2
authnd: kerberos udp 127.0.0.1:18388: listen udp 127.0.0.1:18388: bind: address already in use

Run it as the service account 

sudo -u authnd authnd check /etc/authnd

so that a file only root can read fails here, not at the restart. Run it with the new binary before an upgrade; see install.
